This document contains the analysis scripts and report for the manuscript “A Course on AI for Pre-Service STEM and Language Teachers: A Quasi-Experimental Evaluation of Learning Outcomes Using Intelligent-TPACK and AI Literacy Instruments”. The R scripts, data are hosted at .

1 Methods

1.1 Participants

Code 
data_participants <- data %>%
  filter(time == "pre") %>%
  group_by(intervention, location, gender) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    n_complete = sum(complete.cases(.)),
    age_min = min(age, na.rm = T),
    age_max = max(age, na.rm = T),
    age_mean = mean(age, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    age_sd = sd(age, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    semester_min = min(semester, na.rm = T),
    semester_max = max(semester, na.rm = T),
    semester_mean = mean(semester, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    semester_sd = sd(semester, na.rm = T) %>% round(2)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
`summarise()` has grouped output by 'intervention', 'location'. You can
override using the `.groups` argument.

The study involved pre-service teachers from two universities of education in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. Participants were divided into a treatment group consisting of two intervention groups (STEM and language course), and a control group. Students in the treatment groups self-selected the courses “AI in STEM/Language Education” as part of their compulsory elective studies. The control group was recruited from other STEM courses at University 1 during the same semester.

In total, \(N=145\) students originally participated in the study (\(N_c=59\) in the control group, \(N_s= 50\) in the STEM course, and \(N_l=36\) in the language course), of which \(n=76\) completed both pre- and the posttest and were included in the analyses (\(n_c = 19\), \(n_s = 34\), \(n_l = 23\)).

Unfortunately, we observed a high drop-out rate between the pre- and posttest. We attribute this to several factors: First, the posttests were conducted in class close (one to two weeks) to the examination period, resulting in students not attending the in-person posttest sessions. For the control group, some lecturers executed the posttest during their teaching, while others did not. We suspect a high drop-out at the posttest for the control group due to both factors: students not attending the sessions close to the examination week and not conducting the tests at home or in their free study time.

Descriptive statistics of students’ demographics and pretest scores are presented in Table 1. The final sample size included in the analyses was \(n=76\), aged between \(20\) and \(41\) years (\(M=24.26\), \(SD=4.01\)), of which \(48\) identified as female and \(28\) as male. The students were enrolled in semester \(2\) to \(19\) (\(M=7.46\), \(SD=2.88\)). Of these, \(37\) students were at the Bachelor’s level and \(39\) at the Master’s level.

1.2 Materials

1.2.1 Translation Process

The Intelligent-TPACK, originally developed by Celik (2023), is widely used to assess teachers’ knowledge for pedagogical and ethical AI use based on the technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge (TPACK) framework. However, no empirically validated German translations of the Intelligent-TPACK exists. While some studies translate and use subsets of the Intelligent-TPACK (e.g., Mah & Groß, 2024), there is no validated German version of the full instrument.

Therefore, for the Intelligent-TPACK by Celik (2023) as well as for items from the AI ethics subscale from Chiu et al. (2024), we translated the original items in a participative multi-step process involving not just experts from the fields of computer science and education, but also (pre-service) teachers. For this, we applied the Modified Direct Translation that includes translators and experts discussing the wording until reaching agreement (Behling & Law, 2025): First, seven researchers and experts in AI ED (additionally including one English teacher and one student teacher of Computer Science and English) translated the items independently. Second, we compared all translations and marked the items that received different translations. In a third step, we performed a group workshop with all translators in which the marked items were discussed and dot voting was applied to decide on the most apporopriate translation. Finally, three items that were still marked as questionable were discussed and further adapted with a native English teacher who teaches at University 2.

The translation and validation of the Intelligent-TPACK is reported in detail in Authors (in prep.).

1.3 Analysis

We analyzed the interventions’ efficacy in a multilevel analysis approach. To contrast the differences of students’ change in the respective outcome measure over time, we implemented a linear mixed-effects regression model for each outcome measure, considering our \(3\) factorial design. To account for the panel structure, that is, two test sessions, in the data, we used the random effects (RE) estimation method to estimate treatment effects, following CITATION.

The raw data and R scripts detailing the analyses can be accessed in the online supplement at .

Note

Ist unser Design 3- oder 2-faktoriell?

We implemented the two-level models with the students at level 1 (individual level) and the University at level 2 (class level). We addressed the clustering of time points within students by including random intercepts for students. The clustering of students within universities was addressed by including a dummy variable for the University.

To contrast the differences in change over time between the treatment groups (i.e., estimated treatment effect), we included the time-by-treatment interaction in the models. For this, we used a dummy-coded treatment variable using reversed Helmert contrasts to contrast the differences between (i) the control group and the intervention groups and (ii) between the two intervention groups. We set the control group as the reference group.

Finally, we included variables as a covariate if they met the criteria for baseline equivalence in randomized controlled trials by the What Works Clearinghouse (Clearinghouse, 2022). That is, we included the variables as covariates if the difference between the groups was statistically significant, or if it exceeded \(d>.05\). We tested for group differences concerning the following variables at baseline (pretest): age, gender, semester, and study level (Bachelor vs. Master). We found for gender and semesters statistically significant differences between the treamtment groups, see Table 1. We thus included the following covariates in the models: gender and semester.

That is, the final model for each outcome measure contained time, treatment, gender, semester, University and the interaction of time and treatment as fixed effects and a random intercept for students, and was specified as follows: lmer(outcome ~ time * treatment + gender + semester + university + (1|student)).

The criterion of statistical significance was set at α=.05.

1.3.1 Data Preparation and Cleaning

Code 
# get participants who only participated in pre or post test
data_dropouts <- data_all %>%
  group_by(code) %>%
  summarise(
    has_pre = any(time == "pre"),
    has_post = any(time == "post"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    n_pre_only = sum(has_pre & !has_post),
    n_post_only = sum(!has_pre & has_post),
    n_both = sum(has_pre & has_post)
  )

For data cleaning, we applied the following steps: First, we investigated which students, based on their pseudonyms, did not participate in both test sessions. Based on a string distance analysis using the Levenshtein distance (Levenshtein, 1966), we identified pseudonyms that were likely to belong to the same student but were entered slightly differently (e.g., due to typos or students who moved during the semester, as the address was part of their pseudonym). We then manually checked these pseudonyms and merged them if we believe they belonged to the same student. This resulted in \(n=24\) students being merged. We then removed students who only participated at the pretest (\(n=69\)) or only at the posttest (\(n=11\)). Further, some students conducted the post test twice. In this case, we only considered their first response in the analyses and dropped the second.

As for some self-constructed items students could choose “I don’t understand the item” as a response option, we recoded these responses as missing values (\(n=7\) responses to individual items).

For the Intelligent TPACK, AI ethics and perceived usefulness (sub)scales, we calculated the mean score across all items of the respective (sub)scale per student. For AI literacy, we calculated the sum score across all items. We additionally calculated the sum score for the subset of items of the AI literacy that that directly reflect the topics addressed in the course, see SECTION MATERIALS.

1.3.2 Statistical Software

We performed the statistical analyses in R (R Core Team, 2024) using the following packages: dplyr [wickham2023:dplyr], tidyr (Wickham et al., 2024), and gtools (Warnes et al., 2023) for data wrangling; arsenal (Heinzen et al., 2021), vtable (Huntington-Klein, 2023), modelsummary (Arel-Bundock, 2022) and kableExtra (Zhu, 2024) for creating tables; ggplot2 (Wickham, 2016), ggsci (Xiao, 2024) and jtools (Long, 2022) for plotting; and lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) and lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017) for linear mixed-effects regression analyses.

We used the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) to fit linear mixed-effects models and the broom.mixed package (Bolker & Robinson, 2024) to extract the results. Degrees of freedom and p-values were calculated using the lmerTest package (Kuznetsova et al., 2017) using Kenward-Roger’s approximation for the denominator degrees of freedom. Pairwise comparisons between the treatment groups were computed using the emmeans package (Lenth, 2025).

2 Results

Descriptive statistics of students’ pretest scores are presented in Table 1. As expected, students attending the STEM course and students from the control group, which was recruited from pre-service STEM teachers, reported significantly higher ratings in all Intelligent TPACK subscales compared to students attending language course, which predominantly consisted of students not studying a STEM subject as their second subject. We didn’t find significant differences between the intervention groups for AI literacy, AI ethics, and perceived usefulness at the pretest.

The descriptive statistics of students’ change in the outcome measures over time per treatment group are listed in Figure 1, Figure 2, and Figure 3.

For all outcome measure, we will first report the main treatment effect, i.e., the interaction between time and treatment group. Then, we will report the differences between treatment groups, i.e., control vs. intervention groups (STEM and language course), and then contrast the intervention groups, i.e., STEM vs. language course).

The results of the linear mixed-effects models for each outcome measure are presented in Table 2, Table 3, and Table 4.

2.1 Effect Sizes

Code 
dhat <- function(model, idx = 3, type = 2) {
  f <- abs(tail(summary(model)$coefficients, idx))[1]
  v <- sqrt(tail(anova(model, type = type)[["Mean Sq"]], 1))
  return(f / v)
}
#' Compute standardized effect size d for one fixed effect in an lmer model, based on https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6646942/
#'
#' d = estimate / sqrt(sum of variances of random effects [+ residual if chosen])
#'
#' @param model lmer model
#' @param effect character, name of the fixed effect in fixef(model)
#' @param include_residual logical, include residual variance (default TRUE)
#' @return numeric, effect size d
lmer_d <- function(model, effect, include_residual = TRUE) {
  stopifnot(effect %in% names(lme4::fixef(model)))

  # numerator
  est <- unname(lme4::fixef(model)[effect])

  # variance components
  vc <- as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(model)) # grp, var1, var2, vcov, sdcor
  var_random <- sum(vc$vcov, na.rm = TRUE)

  # residual
  if (!include_residual) {
    var_random <- var_random - sigma(model)^2
  }

  d <- est / sqrt(var_random)
  return(d)
}

effect_sizes_dhat_old <- sapply(lmers_prepost_all, dhat, idx = 2) %>% round(2)

effect_sizes <- sapply(
  lmers_prepost_all,
  lmer_d,
  "intervention-c+STEM_language:time-pre+post"
) %>%
  round(2)
effect_sizes

2.2.1 AI Literacy – Full Scale

We did not find a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change in AI literacy, \(F(2, 73) = 0.95\), \(p = .390\). Neither did the control group’s change differ significantly from both intervention groups, \(b = 1.02\), \(SE = 0.93\), \(t(73.00) = 1.09\), \(p= .277\), nor did the change differ significantly between the two intervention groups, \(b = -0.69\), \(SE = 0.95\), \(t(73.00) = -0.73\), \(p= .467\).

However, as Figure 1 shows, backened by within-group contrast analyses contrasting the AI literacy score between pre- and posttest (see Online Supplement), students in all treatment conditions improved their AI literacy, while the change in pre-service STEM teachers was significant, \(b =1.74\), \(SE = 0.60\), \(t=2.87\), \(p = .005\).

2.2.2 AI Literacy – Study-Specific Subset

For the study-specific subset of the AI literacy items, we also did not find a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change in AI literacy, \(F(2, 73) = 1.45\), \(p = .240\). The control group’s change did not differ significantly from both intervention groups, \(b = 0.89\), \(SE = 0.59\), \(t(73.00) = 1.52\), \(p= .132\), nor did the change between the two intervention groups, \(b = -0.37\), \(SE = 0.60\), \(t(73.00) = -0.61\), \(p= .541\).

However, as can be seen in Figure 1, students in both intervention groups showed descriptively higher increases in AI literacy compared to the control group. When performing post-hoc contrasts, we found that students in the STEM course had a marginally significantly higher increase in the study-specific AI literacy compared to the control group, \(b =1.08\), \(SE = 0.63\), \(t=1.71\), \(p = .092\), while the difference between students in the language course and the control group was insignificant, \(b =0.71\), \(SE = 0.68\), \(t=1.04\), \(p = .301\). All contrast analyses can be accessed in the online supplement at .

2.3 Intelligent TPACK and AI Ethics

The descriptive results of students’ ratings of perceived knowledge in Intelligent TPACK and AI ethics are shown in Figure 2, and Table 3 lists the results of the linear mixed-effects models. As can be seen in Figure 2, all pre-service teachers reported their intelligent TPACK knowledge to be around or below the middle of the scale at the pretest, while the intervention groups reported, on average, values significantly higher than the middle value of the scale at the posttest.

For all subscales related to Intelligent TPACK and AI ethics, that is, Intelligent TK, Intelligent TPK, Intelligent TCK, Intelligent TPACK, and AI ethics, we found a significant main effect of treatment on student’ change on the respective subscales. We found significantly higher increases in students’ Intelligent TPACK subscales in both intervention groups compared to the control group, whereas the intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, see Table 3 for an overview.

2.3.1 Intelligent TK

We found a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change in intelligent TK, \(F(2, 73) = 16.03\), \(p < .001\). We found a significant higher increase in students’ intelligent TK in both intervention groups compared to the control group, \(b = 1.12\), \(SE = 0.20\), \(t(73.00) = 5.66\), \(p< .001\), while the change did not differ significantly between the two intervention groups, \(b = 0.15\), \(SE = 0.20\), \(t(73.00) = 0.72\), \(p= .472\).

2.3.2 Intelligent TPK

We found a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change in intelligent TCK, \(F(2, 73) = 17.03\), \(p < .001\). We found a significant higher increase in students’ intelligent TCK in both intervention groups compared to the control group, \(b = 1.15\), \(SE = 0.20\), \(t(73.00) = 5.82\), \(p< .001\), whereas the two intervention groups did not differ significantly in their change, \(b = 0.19\), \(SE = 0.20\), \(t(73.00) = 0.94\), \(p= .351\).

2.3.3 Intelligent TCK

We found a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change in intelligent TPK, \(F(2, 73) = 11.64\), \(p < .001\). We found a significant higher increase in students’ intelligent TPK in both intervention groups compared to the control group, \(b = 0.95\), \(SE = 0.20\), \(t(73.00) = 4.73\), \(p< .001\), but the change did not differ significantly between the two intervention groups, \(b = -0.10\), \(SE = 0.20\), \(t(73.00) = -0.51\), \(p= .615\).

2.3.4 Intelligent TPACK

For both subscales of the Intelligent TPACK, that is, students’ general TPACK and their perceived competence of applying generative AI in teaching their subject, we found a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change on the respective subscales, TPACK: \(F(2, 73) = 28.24\), \(p < .001\), and TPACK related to generative AI: \(F(2, 73) = 14.00\), \(p < .001\).

For both subscales, we found the same pattern that students’ change in Intelligent TPACK differed significantly between the control group and the two intervention groups, with students in the intervention groups having a significantly higher increase than the control group, whereas the intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other. That is, for TPACK: \(b = 1.38\), \(SE = 0.18\), \(t(73.00) = 7.51\), \(p< .001\) and \(b = 0.09\), \(SE = 0.19\), \(t(73.00) = 0.49\), \(p= .627\); and TPACK related to generative AI, \(b = 1.28\), \(SE = 0.25\), \(t(73.00) = 5.22\), \(p< .001\) and \(b = 0.09\), \(SE = 0.19\), \(t(73.00) = 0.49\), \(p= .627\).

2.3.5 AI Ethics

For ethics related to the use of AI in education, we found a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change in XYZ, \(F(2, 73) = 16.55\), \(p < .001\). We found a significant higher increase in students’ XYZ in the intervention groups compared to the control group, \(b = 1.41\), \(SE = 0.25\), \(t(73.00) = 5.72\), \(p< .001\), whereas the change did not differ significantly between the two intervention groups, \(b = 0.30\), \(SE = 0.25\), \(t(73.00) = 1.22\), \(p= .228\).

2.4 Perceived Usefulness

Descriptive results of students’ perceived usefulness of XYZ are listed in Figure 3, while the results of the linear mixed-effects models for perceived usefulness are presented in Table 4.

For the overall perceived usefulness, we did not find a significant main effect of treatment on students’ change in perceived usefulness, \(F(2, 73) = 1.74\), \(p = .182\). Neither did the control group’s change differ significantly from both intervention groups, \(b = 0.28\), \(SE = 0.17\), \(t(73.00) = 1.65\), \(p= .103\), nor did the change differ significantly between the two intervention groups, \(b = -0.12\), \(SE = 0.17\), \(t(73.00) = -0.71\), \(p= .482\).

However, when investigating the individual items of perceived usefulness, we found that students in the intervention groups showed marginally significant higher increases compared to the control group, \(b = 0.48\), \(SE = 0.28\), \(t(73.00) = 1.71\), \(p= .091\) and \(b = 0.54\), \(SE = 0.29\), \(t(73.00) = 1.87\), \(p= .065\), whereas the change did not differ significantly between the two intervention groups, \(b = -0.08\), \(SE = 0.29\), \(t(73.00) = -0.26\), \(p= .793\) and \(b = 0.37\), \(SE = 0.30\), \(t(73.00) = 1.27\), \(p= .208\), respectively, whereas we found no treatment effect for PU3 and PU4, see Table 4.

4.2 Demographics Check

Code 
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

check_demo_vars <- function(
  data,
  demo_vars = c("age", "semester", "gender", "students"),
  id = "code",
  time_col = "time",
  pre_label = "pre",
  post_label = "post",
  show_only_diff = FALSE
) {
  out <- data %>%
    select(all_of(c(id, time_col, demo_vars))) %>%
    # ensure a common type across demo vars
    mutate(across(all_of(demo_vars), as.character)) %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols = all_of(demo_vars),
      names_to = "variable",
      values_to = "value"
      # alternatively: values_transform = as.character
      # or: values_ptypes = list(value = character())
    ) %>%
    group_by(.data[[id]], variable, .data[[time_col]]) %>%
    summarise(
      value = paste(unique(na.omit(value)), collapse = ", "),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = all_of(time_col), values_from = value) %>%
    transmute(
      !!id := .data[[id]],
      variable,
      pre = .data[[pre_label]],
      post = .data[[post_label]],
      match = (pre == post) | (is.na(pre) & is.na(post))
    ) %>%
    arrange(.data[[id]], variable)

  if (show_only_diff) {
    out <- filter(out, is.na(match) | !match)
  }
  out
}
check_demo_vars(
  data,
  demo_vars = c(
    "age",
    "semester",
    "gender",
    "students",
    "intervention",
    "location"
  ),
  id = "code",
  show_only_diff = T
)

data_wtf <- data %>%
  droplevels %>%
  mutate(
    location = factor(
      location,
      levels = c("PH Schwäbisch Gmünd", "PH Ludwigsburg")
    )
  )

## define contrast Control vs Exp1+Exp2 - vermutlich bessere version, da die Estimates "stimmen"
mat <- cbind(
  c(1 / 3, 1 / 3, 1 / 3), # Durchschnitt aller 3 Gruppen
  c(-1, .5, .5), # Vergleich Control vs Mittel der beiden Interventions-Gruppen
  c(0, -1, 1)
) # Vergleich Sprache vs MINT
contrasts.CvsExp <- solve(t(mat))[, -1]
colnames(contrasts.CvsExp) <- c("-c+STEM_language", "-STEM+language")
contrasts(data_wtf$intervention) <- contrasts.CvsExp

# GENDER
# female: -1/2
# male : +1/2
contrasts.gender <- cbind(c(-1 / 2, 1 / 2))
colnames(contrasts.gender) <- c("-m+f")
contrasts(data_wtf$gender) <- contrasts.gender

# LOCATION

# L UE: +1/2

contrasts(data_wtf$location) <- contrasts.location

# TIME
# pre: -1/2
# post: +1/2
contrasts.time <- cbind(c(-1 / 2, 1 / 2))
colnames(contrasts.time) <- c("-pre+post")
contrasts(data_wtf$time) <- contrasts.time

data <- data_wtf
# refit all lmer_prepost_all with new data
lmers_prepost_all <- lapply(
  outcomes,
  fit_lmer,

  time,
  controls,
  random_terms_lmer,
  NULL,
  data = data
)
names(lmers_prepost_all) <- outcomes

# Methods

## Participants

```{r}
data_participants <- data %>%
  filter(time == "pre") %>%
  group_by(intervention, location, gender) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    n_complete = sum(complete.cases(.)),
    age_min = min(age, na.rm = T),
    age_max = max(age, na.rm = T),
    age_mean = mean(age, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    age_sd = sd(age, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    semester_min = min(semester, na.rm = T),
    semester_max = max(semester, na.rm = T),
    semester_mean = mean(semester, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    semester_sd = sd(semester, na.rm = T) %>% round(2)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```


The study involved pre-service teachers from two universities of education in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. Participants were divided into a **treatment group** consisting of two intervention groups (STEM and language course), and a **control group**.
Students in the treatment groups self-selected the courses "AI in STEM/Language Education" as part of their compulsory elective studies. The control group was recruited from other STEM courses at University 1 during the same semester. 

In total, $N=`r data_all %>% filter(time=="pre") %>% nrow()`$ students originally participated in the study ($N_c=`r data_all %>% filter(time=="pre", intervention=="control") %>%nrow`$ in the control group, $N_s= `r data_all %>% filter(time=="pre", intervention=="stem") %>%nrow `$ in the STEM course, and $N_l=`r data_all %>% filter(time=="pre", intervention=="language") %>%nrow `$ in the language course), of which $n=`r data_participants$n %>% sum`$ completed both pre- and the posttest and were included in the analyses ($n_c = `r data_participants%>%filter(intervention=="control") %>% select(n)%>%sum`$, $n_s = `r data_participants%>%filter(intervention=="stem") %>% select(n)%>%sum`$, $n_l = `r data_participants%>%filter(intervention=="language") %>% select(n) %>% sum`$).

Unfortunately, we observed a high drop-out rate between the pre- and posttest. We attribute this to several factors: First, the posttests were conducted in class close  (one to two weeks) to the examination period, resulting in students not attending the in-person posttest sessions. For the control group, some lecturers executed the posttest during their teaching, while others did not. We suspect a high drop-out at the posttest for the control group due to both factors: students not attending the sessions close to the examination week and not conducting the tests at home or in their free study time.


Descriptive statistics of students' demographics and pretest scores are presented in [@tbl-participants]. The final sample size included in the analyses was $n=76$, aged between $`r data_pre$age%>%min`$ and $`r data_pre$age %>% max`$ years ($M=`r data_pre$age%>%mean %>% round(2)`$, $SD=`r data_pre$age%>%sd%>%round(2)`$), of which $`r data_pre%>%filter(gender=="Weiblich")%>%nrow`$ identified as female and $`r data_pre%>%filter(gender=="Männlich")%>%nrow`$ as male.
The students were enrolled in semester $`r data_pre$semester%>%min`$ to $`r data_pre$semester%>%max`$ ($M=`r data_pre$semester%>%mean%>%round(2)`$, $SD=`r data_pre$semester%>%sd%>%round(2)`$). Of these, $`r data_pre%>%filter(students=="bachelor")%>%nrow`$ students were at the Bachelor's level and $`r data_pre%>%filter(students=="master")%>%nrow`$ at the Master's level.

## Materials

### Translation Process
The Intelligent-TPACK, originally developed by @celik2023, is widely used to assess teachers’ knowledge for pedagogical and ethical AI use based on the technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge (TPACK) framework.
However, no empirically validated German translations of the Intelligent-TPACK exists. While some studies translate and use subsets of the Intelligent-TPACK [e.g., @mah.gross2024], there is no validated German version of the full instrument. 

Therefore, for the Intelligent-TPACK by @celik2023 as well as for items from the AI ethics subscale from @chiu.ahmad.ea2024, we translated the original items in a participative multi-step process involving not just experts from the fields of computer science and education, but also (pre-service) teachers.
For this, we applied the *Modified Direct Translation* that includes translators and experts discussing the wording until reaching agreement [@behling.law2025]: First, seven researchers and experts in AI ED (additionally including one English teacher and one student teacher of Computer Science and English) translated the items independently. Second, we compared all translations and marked the items that received different translations. In a third step, we performed a group workshop with all translators in which the marked items were discussed and dot voting was applied to decide on the most apporopriate translation. Finally, three items that were still marked as questionable were discussed and further adapted with a native English teacher who teaches at University 2.

The translation and validation of the Intelligent-TPACK is reported in detail in @authorsinprep.

## Analysis
We analyzed the interventions' efficacy in a multilevel analysis approach. To contrast the differences of students' change in the respective outcome measure over time, we implemented a linear mixed-effects regression model for each outcome measure, considering our $3$ factorial design. To account for the panel structure, that is, two test sessions, in the data, we used the random effects (RE) estimation method to estimate treatment effects, following CITATION.

The raw data and *R* scripts detailing the analyses can be accessed in the online supplement at <OSF>.

:::{.callout-note}
Ist unser Design 3- oder 2-faktoriell?
:::

We implemented the two-level models with the students at level 1 (individual level) and the University at level 2 (class level). We addressed the clustering of time points within students by including random intercepts for students. The clustering of students within universities was addressed by including a dummy variable for the University. 

To contrast the differences in change over time between the treatment groups (i.e., estimated treatment effect), we included the time-by-treatment interaction in the models. For this, we used a dummy-coded *treatment* variable using reversed Helmert contrasts to contrast the differences between (i) the *control* group and the *intervention* groups and (ii) between the two intervention groups. We set the control group as the reference group.

Finally, we included variables as a covariate if they met the criteria for baseline equivalence in randomized controlled trials by the What Works Clearinghouse [@WWC2022]. That is, we included the variables as covariates if the difference between the groups was statistically significant, or if it exceeded $d>.05$.
We tested for group differences concerning the following variables at baseline (pretest): age, gender, semester, and study level (Bachelor vs. Master). We found for gender and semesters  statistically significant differences between the treamtment groups, see [@tbl-participants]. We thus included the following covariates in the models: gender and semester.

That is, the final model for each outcome measure contained time, treatment, gender, semester, University and the interaction of time and treatment as fixed effects and a random intercept for students, and was specified as follows:
`lmer(outcome ~ time * treatment + gender + semester + university + (1|student))`.

The criterion of statistical significance was set at α=.05.

### Data Preparation and Cleaning


```{r}
# get participants who only participated in pre or post test
data_dropouts <- data_all %>%
  group_by(code) %>%
  summarise(
    has_pre = any(time == "pre"),
    has_post = any(time == "post"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    n_pre_only = sum(has_pre & !has_post),
    n_post_only = sum(!has_pre & has_post),
    n_both = sum(has_pre & has_post)
  )
```

For data cleaning, we applied the following steps: First, we investigated which students, based on their pseudonyms, did not participate in both test sessions. Based on a string distance analysis using the Levenshtein distance [@levenshtein1966], we identified pseudonyms that were likely to belong to the same student but were entered slightly differently (e.g., due to typos or students who moved during the semester, as the address was part of their pseudonym). We then manually checked these pseudonyms and merged them if we believe they belonged to the same student. This resulted in $n=24$ students being merged.
We then removed students who only participated at the pretest ($n=`r data_dropouts$n_pre_only`$) or only at the posttest ($n=`r data_dropouts$n_post_only`$).
Further, some students conducted the post test twice. In this case, we only considered their first response in the analyses and dropped the second.

As for some self-constructed items students could choose "I don't understand the item" as a response option, we recoded these responses as missing values ($n=`r data %>%
  select(all_of(c(list_items_i_tpack, list_items_pu)%>%unlist)) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) %>% sum`$ responses to individual items).

For the Intelligent TPACK, AI ethics and perceived usefulness (sub)scales, we calculated the mean score across all items of the respective (sub)scale per student. For AI literacy, we calculated the sum score across all items. We additionally calculated the sum score for the subset of items of the AI literacy   that that directly reflect the topics addressed in the course, see SECTION MATERIALS.

### Statistical Software
We performed the statistical analyses in *R* [@R2024] using the following packages:
*dplyr* [wickham2023:dplyr], *tidyr* [@wickham2024], and *gtools* [@warnes2023] for data wrangling;
*arsenal* [@heinzen2021], *vtable* [@huntington2023], *modelsummary* [@arel-bundock2022] and *kableExtra* [@zhu2024] for creating tables; *ggplot2* [@wickham2016], *ggsci* [@xiao2024] and *jtools* [@long2022] for plotting; and *lme4* [@bates2015] and *lmerTest* [@kuznetsova2017] for linear mixed-effects regression analyses.

We used the *lme4* package [@bates2015] to fit linear mixed-effects models and the *broom.mixed* package [@bolker2024] to extract the results. Degrees of freedom and *p*-values were calculated using the *lmerTest* package [@kuznetsova2017] using Kenward-Roger's approximation for the denominator degrees of freedom. Pairwise comparisons between the treatment groups were computed using the *emmeans* package [@lenth2025].


# Results

Descriptive statistics of students' pretest scores are presented in [@tbl-participants].
As expected, students attending the STEM course and students from the control group, which was recruited from pre-service STEM teachers, reported significantly higher ratings in all Intelligent TPACK subscales compared to students attending language course, which predominantly consisted of students not studying a STEM subject as their second subject. We didn't find significant differences between the intervention groups for AI literacy, AI ethics, and perceived usefulness at the pretest.

The descriptive statistics of students' change in the outcome measures over time per treatment group are listed in  [@fig-ai-lit], [@fig-tpack], and [@fig-pu].

For all outcome measure, we will first report the *main* treatment effect, i.e., the interaction between time and treatment group. Then, we will report the differences between treatment groups, i.e., control vs. intervention groups (STEM and language course), and then contrast the intervention groups, i.e., STEM vs. language course).

The results of the linear mixed-effects models for each outcome measure are presented in [@tbl-lmer-ailit-summary], [@tbl-lmer-tpack-summary], and [@tbl-lmer-pu-summary].

## Effect Sizes

```{r effect-sizes}
dhat <- function(model, idx = 3, type = 2) {
  f <- abs(tail(summary(model)$coefficients, idx))[1]
  v <- sqrt(tail(anova(model, type = type)[["Mean Sq"]], 1))
  return(f / v)
}
#' Compute standardized effect size d for one fixed effect in an lmer model, based on https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6646942/
#'
#' d = estimate / sqrt(sum of variances of random effects [+ residual if chosen])
#'
#' @param model lmer model
#' @param effect character, name of the fixed effect in fixef(model)
#' @param include_residual logical, include residual variance (default TRUE)
#' @return numeric, effect size d
lmer_d <- function(model, effect, include_residual = TRUE) {
  stopifnot(effect %in% names(lme4::fixef(model)))

  # numerator
  est <- unname(lme4::fixef(model)[effect])

  # variance components
  vc <- as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(model)) # grp, var1, var2, vcov, sdcor
  var_random <- sum(vc$vcov, na.rm = TRUE)

  # residual
  if (!include_residual) {
    var_random <- var_random - sigma(model)^2
  }

  d <- est / sqrt(var_random)
  return(d)
}

effect_sizes_dhat_old <- sapply(lmers_prepost_all, dhat, idx = 2) %>% round(2)

effect_sizes <- sapply(
  lmers_prepost_all,
  lmer_d,
  "intervention-c+STEM_language:time-pre+post"
) %>%
  round(2)
effect_sizes
```

### AI Literacy -- Full Scale
We did not find a significant main effect of treatment on students' change in AI literacy, `r report_lmer_anova(lmers_prepost_all[["AILIT"]])`. Neither did the control group's change differ significantly from both intervention groups, 
`r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["AILIT"]], term = tc1)`, nor did the change differ significantly between the two intervention groups, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["AILIT"]], term = tc2)`.

However, as [@fig-ai-lit] shows, backened by within-group contrast analyses contrasting the AI literacy score between pre- and posttest (see Online Supplement), students in all treatment conditions improved their AI literacy, while the change in pre-service STEM teachers was significant, `r report_contrast(ailit_within_contrasts[[1]], 2)`.

### AI Literacy -- Study-Specific Subset
For the study-specific subset of the AI literacy items, we also did not find a significant main effect of treatment on students' change in AI literacy, `r report_lmer_anova(lmers_prepost_all[["AILITWolke"]])`. The control group's change did not differ significantly from both intervention groups, 
`r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["AILITWolke"]], term = tc1)`, nor did the change between the two intervention groups, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["AILITWolke"]], term = tc2)`.

```{r, results="asis"}
if (!is_word) {
  cat("#### Pairwise Contrasts Within Groups")
}
```

```{r ailit-within-contrasts}

# pairwise within contrasts (no multiplicity adjustment)
ailit_within_contrasts <- lapply(lmers_prepost_all[1:3], function(m) {
  emmeans(m, ~ time | intervention) %>%
    contrast(method = "revpairwise", adjust = "none")
})
if (!is_word) {
  print(ailit_within_contrasts)
}
```

```{r, results="asis"}
if (!is_word) {
  cat("#### Pairwise Contrasts Between Groups")
}
```

```{r ailit-between-contrasts}
# pairwise between contrasts (no multiplicity adjustment)
ailit_between_contrasts <- lapply(lmers_prepost_all[1:3], function(m) {
  emmeans(m, ~ intervention * time) %>%
    contrast(interaction = "revpairwise", adjust = "none")
})
if (!is_word) {
  print(ailit_between_contrasts)
}
```

However, as can be seen in [@fig-ai-lit], students in both intervention groups showed descriptively higher increases in AI literacy compared to the control group. When performing post-hoc contrasts, we found that students in the STEM course had a marginally significantly higher increase in the study-specific AI literacy compared to the control group, `r report_contrast(ailit_between_contrasts[[2]], 1)`, while the difference between students in the language course and the control group was insignificant, `r report_contrast(ailit_between_contrasts[[2]],2)`. All contrast analyses can be accessed in the online supplement at <OSF>.


## Intelligent TPACK and AI Ethics
The descriptive results of students' ratings of perceived knowledge in Intelligent TPACK and AI ethics are shown in [@fig-tpack], and [@tbl-lmer-tpack-summary] lists the results of the linear mixed-effects models. As can be seen in [@fig-tpack], all pre-service teachers reported their intelligent TPACK knowledge to be around or below the middle of the scale at the pretest, while the intervention groups reported, on average, values significantly higher than the middle value of the scale at the posttest.

For all subscales related to Intelligent TPACK and AI ethics, that is, Intelligent TK, Intelligent TPK, Intelligent TCK, Intelligent TPACK, and AI ethics, we found a significant main effect of treatment on student' change on the respective subscales. We found significantly higher increases in students' Intelligent TPACK subscales in both intervention groups compared to the control group, whereas the intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, see [@tbl-lmer-tpack-summary] for an overview.

```{r fig-tpack, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Descriptive Statistics of Students' Intelligent TPACK and AI Ethics Ratings Over Time by Treatment Group.", out.width="100%",fig.width=7, fig.height=6.5}
p_tpack +
  facet_wrap(
    ~outcome,
    scales = "fixed",
    ncol = 3,
    labeller = labeller(
      outcome = c(
        TK = "Intelligent TK",
        TCK = "Intelligent TCK",
        TPK = "Intelligent TPK",
        TPACKce = "Intelligent TPACK - Core",
        TPACKgenai = "iTPACK - Generative AI",
        Ethics = "AI Ethics"
      )
    )
  ) +
  ggtitle("Intelligent TPACK and AI Ethics") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

:::

### Intelligent TK
We found a significant main effect of treatment on students' change in intelligent TK, `r report_lmer_anova(lmers_prepost_all[["TK"]])`. 
We found a significant higher increase in students' intelligent TK in both intervention groups compared to the control group, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["TK"]], term = tc1)`, while the change did not differ significantly between the two intervention groups, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["TK"]], term = tc2)`.

### Intelligent TPK
We found a significant main effect of treatment on students' change in intelligent TCK, `r report_lmer_anova(lmers_prepost_all[["TPK"]])`.
We found a significant higher increase in students' intelligent TCK in both intervention groups compared to the control group, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["TPK"]], term = tc1)`, whereas the two intervention groups did not differ significantly in their change, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["TPK"]], term = tc2)`.

### Intelligent TCK
We found a significant main effect of treatment on students' change in intelligent TPK, `r report_lmer_anova(lmers_prepost_all[["TCK"]])`.
We found a significant higher increase in students' intelligent TPK in both intervention groups compared to the control group, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["TCK"]], term = tc1)`, but the change did not differ significantly between the two intervention groups, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["TCK"]], term = tc2)`.

### Intelligent TPACK
For both subscales of the Intelligent TPACK, that is, students' general TPACK and their perceived competence of applying *generative AI* in teaching their subject, we found a significant main effect of treatment on students' change on the respective subscales, *TPACK*: `r report_lmer_anova(lmers_prepost_all[["TPACKce"]])`, and *TPACK related to generative AI*: `r report_lmer_anova(lmers_prepost_all[["TPACKgenai"]])`.

For both subscales, we found the same pattern that students' change in Intelligent TPACK differed significantly between the control group and the two intervention groups, with students in the intervention groups having a significantly higher increase than the control group, whereas the intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other. That is, for *TPACK*:  `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["TPACKce"]], term = tc1)` and `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["TPACKce"]], term = tc2)`; and *TPACK related to generative AI*, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["TPACKgenai"]], term = tc1)` and `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[[7]], term = tc2)`.

### AI Ethics
For ethics related to the use of AI in education, we found a significant main effect of treatment on students' change in **XYZ**, `r report_lmer_anova(lmers_prepost_all[["Ethics"]])`. We found a significant higher increase in students' **XYZ** in the intervention groups compared to the control group, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["Ethics"]], term = tc1)`, whereas the change did not differ significantly between the two intervention groups, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["Ethics"]], term = tc2)`.

:::

For the overall perceived usefulness, we did not find a significant main effect of treatment on students' change in perceived usefulness, `r report_lmer_anova(lmers_prepost_all[["PU"]])`. Neither did the control group's change differ significantly from both intervention groups, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["PU"]], term = tc1)`, nor did the change differ significantly between the two intervention groups, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["PU"]], term = tc2)`.

However, when investigating the individual items of perceived usefulness, we found that students in the intervention groups showed marginally significant higher increases compared to the control group, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["PU1"]], term = tc1)` and `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["PU2"]], term = tc1)`, whereas the change did not differ significantly between the two intervention groups, `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["PU1"]], term = tc2)` and `r report_lmer(lmers_prepost_all[["PU2"]], term = tc2)`, respectively, whereas we found no treatment effect for *PU3*  and *PU4*, see [@tbl-lmer-pu-summary].

## Demographics Check
```{r test}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

check_demo_vars <- function(
  data,
  demo_vars = c("age", "semester", "gender", "students"),
  id = "code",
  time_col = "time",
  pre_label = "pre",
  post_label = "post",
  show_only_diff = FALSE
) {
  out <- data %>%
    select(all_of(c(id, time_col, demo_vars))) %>%
    # ensure a common type across demo vars
    mutate(across(all_of(demo_vars), as.character)) %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols = all_of(demo_vars),
      names_to = "variable",
      values_to = "value"
      # alternatively: values_transform = as.character
      # or: values_ptypes = list(value = character())
    ) %>%
    group_by(.data[[id]], variable, .data[[time_col]]) %>%
    summarise(
      value = paste(unique(na.omit(value)), collapse = ", "),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = all_of(time_col), values_from = value) %>%
    transmute(
      !!id := .data[[id]],
      variable,
      pre = .data[[pre_label]],
      post = .data[[post_label]],
      match = (pre == post) | (is.na(pre) & is.na(post))
    ) %>%
    arrange(.data[[id]], variable)

  if (show_only_diff) {
    out <- filter(out, is.na(match) | !match)
  }
  out
}
check_demo_vars(
  data,
  demo_vars = c(
    "age",
    "semester",
    "gender",
    "students",
    "intervention",
    "location"
  ),
  id = "code",
  show_only_diff = T
)
```
